title: We Do Not Know How to Say Goodbye
text:
We do not know how to say goodbye:

we wander about, shoulder to shoulder.

Already the sun is setting,

you go taciturn, I am your shadow.


Let us go into a church to see

baptisms, weddings, funeral masses.

Why are we different from the rest?

Outside again, each one turns their head.


Or let us sit in the cemetery,

on the trampled snow, sighing for one another.

That rod in your hand is drawing mansions

where we will always be together.




1917
editorial_note: The translation keeps the lovers' inability to part and the imagined mansions drawn in cemetery snow.

title: They Must Have Shown You—Mocking
text:
They must have shown you—mocking,

delight of your friends, thief of hearts,

the naughtiest girl in Pushkin's town—

this photograph of your calamitous years,

how you stand beside a hostile wall,

among three hundred ragged ones in line,

taking a ration in your hand

and the New Year's ice reduced to embers by your tears.

Look at the prison poplar bending!

No noise. Not a sound. Even so, how many

innocent lives are ending.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the contrast between youthful mockery and the prison-line photograph.

title: I Wrung My Hands
text:
I wrung my hands beneath my dark veil.

"Why are you pale, what troubles you?"

"Because I made my beloved drunk

with a hidden sadness."


I will never forget it. He went out staggering:

his mouth twisted, desolate...

I ran down the stairs, without touching the banisters,

after him, to the door.


And I shouted to him, shaken: "Everything I said

was in jest; do not leave me, or I will die of grief."

He smiled at me, terribly slowly,

and exclaimed: "Why don't you get out of the rain?"




1911
editorial_note: The translation keeps the dramatic exchange and the chillingly ordinary final question.

title: Everything Has Been Plundered
text:
Everything has been plundered, betrayed, sold.

The great black wings of death rip the air,

Misery gnaws to the bone.

How, then, not despair?


During the day, from nearby woods,

the cherries carry summer into the city.

At night, the deep transparent skies

shine with new galaxies.


And the miraculous approaches, imminent,

to the filthy ruined houses—

something that in fact no one knows,

though wild in our breast for centuries.




1921
editorial_note: The translation keeps the movement from devastation to the inexplicable nearness of the miraculous.

title: I Came to Visit the Poet
text:
I came to visit the poet

exactly at noon, on a Sunday.

In the spacious room silence reigned;

outside, in the street, it was cold.


A pleasant sun wandered

over the thick blue-gray smoke...

The poet looked at me fixedly,

in silence, like a great host.


It is better to be careful

and never look into his eyes;

they are such strange eyes

that they can never be forgotten.


I will not forget that meeting,

that misty Sunday noon

on the banks of the Neva

in a large gray house.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the quiet visit, strange gaze, and gray Neva setting.

title: Everything Has Been Taken from Me
text:
Everything has been taken from me: love and strength.

My body, hurled into a city I detest,

does not rejoice even in the sun. I feel that my blood

is frozen.


I am mocked by the mood of the Muse

who watches me and says nothing,

resting her head of dark curls,

exhausted, on my breast.


Only Conscience, more terrible each day,

enraged, demands a great tribute.

And to answer, I cover my face with my hands,

because I have exhausted my tears and my excuses.




1916
editorial_note: The translation preserves the speaker's stripped condition and the silent, exhausted Muse.

title: For Seventeen Months I Have Screamed
text:
For seventeen months I have screamed,

calling you back to the fold.

I threw myself at the executioner's feet.

You are my son, turned specter.

Confusion seizes the world

and I lack the strength to distinguish

between a beast and a human being,

or on what day the word kill! is spelled out.

Nothing remains but dusty flowers,

a tinkling censer and footprints

that lead nowhere. Stone night,

whose bright and gigantic star

stares into my eyes,

promising me death. Ah, soon!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the motherly desperation, failed distinctions, and stone-night death promise.

title: What Lives Here Will Live Longer than I...
text:
What lives here will live longer than I,

even the starlings' nests,

and this migratory air that crossed,

spring air, the sea in flight.


Eternity's voice calls us from there,

from beyond with its invincible force,

and above the cherry tree in bloom,

the waning moonlight pours down.


It seems to whiten without hindrance,

through the green thickets,

the path I do not say where it leads...


There is more clarity among the trunks

and everything resembles the grove

that surrounds the pond in Tsarskoye Selo.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the survival of place, migratory air, and the remembered Tsarskoye Selo grove.

title: There Is in Intimacy a Sacred Limit
text:
There is in intimacy a sacred limit

that even the maddest passion cannot cross,

even if love tears the heart

and in the midst of silence our mouths melt together.


Friendship can do nothing, years can do nothing,

of high flights, of flaming bliss,

when the soul is free and is not conquered

by the sweet languor of pleasure and lust.


Deranged minds seek to reach it,

and those who cross it are filled with sadness.

Do you understand now why my heart

does not beat in rhythm beneath your right hand?
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sacred boundary inside intimacy and the final embodied proof of distance.

title: Prologue
text:
It was an age when only the dead

could smile, freed from wars;

and the emblem, the soul of Leningrad,

hung outside its prison-house;

and the armies of captives,

herded in the railroad yards,

escaped from the song sung by the whistle of the

engine,

whose refrain went: Go away, pariahs!

The stars of death hung above us.

And Russia, the innocent, the beloved, writhed

under the tracks of boots stained with blood,

under the wheels of the Black Marias.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the Requiem prologue's historical scale, prison-house image, and Black Maria vans.
